newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish foreign minister leaves on Mideast trip.
newsitem.headline: Irish foreign minister leaves on Mideast trip.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring left Dublin for Israel on Sunday to secure a role for the European Union in the faltering Middle East peace process.
"The EU wants me to take a strong message to the Israelis and Palestinians that Europe wants to see the Middle East peace accords respected," Spring said on departure.
Spring, whose country holds the current EU presidency, was expected to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later in the day after arriving in Tel Aviv, officials said.

Spring, responding to Israeli and U.S. concern about EU criticism of Israel, promised he would be even-handed but said Netanyahu's government could make a gesture which would restore the 1993 Middle East peace pacts.
"I think there is plenty of room for inititiative to be taken by the Israeli government," he told Irish radio.

Spring said an Israeli withdrawal from Hebron, as stipulated in the peace accords, was one possible gesture and said he would also be discussing the opening of a tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem which sparked the current crisis.
But the Israeli government also had "legitimate concerns about security which have to be addressed," he said.
"I want to be even-handed," said Spring, whose hastily- arranged trip was mandated by an EU summit which ended late on Saturday night.
Spring declined to say whether he intended a potentially fraught visit to meet Palestinian Authority officials in their Orient House offices in East Jerusalem.
The Netanyahu government has told Spring it would frown upon such a plan out of fear that it would be seen as support for Palestinian claims to Jerusalem.
"Details of the visit have yet to be fixed. I am going to talk to Mr. Netanyahu first," Spring said.
He was also expected to confer with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher who is to attend talks between Israelis and Palestinians on the Israeli border.
Irish officials said talks with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat were also probable but exact details of the hastily- arranged visit had yet to be fixed.
It was not known how long Spring would stay in the region but his attendance at U.S. talks in Pittsburgh on investment for Northern Ireland on Monday was cancelled, officials said.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said late on Saturday that the EU was the biggest aid donor to the region and had a role to play in reviving the peace process.
His remarks echoed concern among many European capitals that the European Union had been sidelined in U.S.-led attempts to get 1993 Middle East peace accords back on track.
Arafat appealed this week for more EU involvement in efforts to patch up the peace process.

But some EU officials in Dublin said the U.S. had shown opposition to a greater European role and was concerned that the EU should demonstrate an even-handed approach between the Israeli and Palestinian positions.
Diplomats said they had been told that Christopher had sent a letter to the EU which appeared to suggest it should not become too involved.
